label: Conflict With Others
framing: Conflict is not a sign that something has gone wrong with you. Scripture assumes it will come even among people who love each other, and it refuses both the avoidance that buries the wound and the explosion that widens it.
cultural: In the honor-shame world of the New Testament, a public dispute was a contest over standing, and to back down was to lose face before the watching community. Into that, Jesus told the offended party to go privately first, sparing the other person's honor, and Paul told a small church that their lawsuits against one another were already a defeat before any verdict came down.
historical: The church wrote its first rules for handling conflict early, building Matthew 18 into the way communities confronted and restored one another. Benedict in the sixth century ordered his monks to reconcile before sundown, the Anabaptists made the hard private conversation a mark of the church, and across history the wise have insisted that peacemaking is not the absence of conflict but the costly work of going through it.
application: Go to the person directly and privately before you go to anyone else, which spares their dignity and your own. Name the specific wrong rather than their whole character, and own your part of it honestly. Aim at the restored relationship, not at winning the point. And where you can, be the one who absorbs the small offense rather than litigating it, for it is a glory to overlook an offense.

verses.text: What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the passions at war within you?
verses.where: James asks what causes the conflicts and quarrels among his readers, and answers his own question: the passions at war within them. The site's note says he traces their quarrels to disordered desires. Before a fight is about the other person, it is usually about something we want badly and are not getting.

verses.text: To start a quarrel is to release a flood; so abandon the dispute before it breaks out.
verses.where: Proverbs compares starting a quarrel to releasing a flood, and counsels dropping the dispute before it breaks out. The site's note says the chapter dwells on the damage of quarrels and prefers a dry crust in peace to a feast full of strife. Once water is through the dam, no one controls where it goes.

verses.text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
verses.where: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The site's note says the chapter opens with this saying and keeps returning to the tongue, soothing or perverse, timely or rash. Gentleness here is not weakness; it is the strength that keeps a disagreement from becoming a war.

verses.text: My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.
verses.where: James tells everyone to be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to anger, because human anger does not bring about the righteousness God desires. The site's note sets it beside James's call to be doers of the word, whose religion shows in controlled speech. Most conflicts would change if each side listened before it answered.

verses.text: Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but fail to notice the beam in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ while there is still a beam in your own eye? You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.
verses.where: Jesus draws a comic picture of a man with a beam in his own eye offering to remove a speck from his brother's. The site's note says verse 5 does not forbid helping the brother; it sets the order: first your own eye, then you will see clearly enough to help. In a conflict, the first question is what you contributed to it.

verses.text: A man’s insight gives him patience, and his virtue is to overlook an offense.
verses.where: A person's insight gives him patience, and his virtue is to overlook an offense. Not every wrong needs a confrontation; many are better absorbed than answered. The site's notes elsewhere are just as clear that this never means keeping silent about abuse or crime, which are another matter entirely.

verses.text: Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is a passerby who meddles in a quarrel not his own.
verses.where: Meddling in a quarrel that is not yours is like grabbing a passing dog by the ears. The site's note says these verses expose the meddler, the gossip and the quarreler. Some conflicts are yours to help with, and some are yours to stay out of, and wisdom learns the difference.

verses.text: He moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. He named it Rehoboth and said, “At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.”
verses.where: When the herdsmen of Gerar quarrel with Isaac's servants over one well and then another, Isaac moves on and digs a third, and this time there is no quarrel; he names it Rehoboth, room. The site's note says he names each place after what happened there, and that this is his first speech in the chapter not about fear, giving the LORD the credit for the space. Sometimes peace is found by making room rather than winning the argument.

verses.text: So then, let us pursue what leads to peace and to mutual edification.
verses.where: Writing to believers divided over food and holy days, Paul tells them to pursue what leads to peace and to building one another up. The site's note says he will not let either side look down on or condemn the other, because God has welcomed both. Many conflicts among Christians are over matters on which both sides can stand before the Lord.

verses.text: Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen.
verses.where: Paul tells believers to let no unwholesome talk come out of their mouths, but only what builds up the one in need and gives grace to those who listen. The site's note says the new life shows in truthful speech, controlled anger and words that build up. The test of a hard conversation is not whether you won it but whether your words were true and gave grace.

misread.taken: Restore him with a spirit of gentleness is sometimes used to keep a serious wrong quiet, to tell the people who were hurt to say nothing, or to put someone who harmed others straight back into a place of trust.
misread.says: The site's plain note says Paul is speaking of bringing back a believer overtaken by sin, humbly and kindly, and that churches should practice it. But it says plainly that the verse has been misused in exactly this way, and that this is not what Paul means. Restoring a person to Christ is not the same as restoring them to a position of trust, and gentleness toward the one who fell never means carelessness toward the ones who were hurt. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities.
misread.text: Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted.

whole: If a conflict has turned into threats, harassment or violence, at work, at home, in a neighborhood or in a church, your safety comes first: tell someone you trust and get help, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Most conflict is less dangerous than that, and still exhausting. A coworker who takes credit or undercuts you. A neighbor and a fence line. A friend who said something careless and will not see it. A ministry team split over decisions. Family group chats that turn sharp. Some people avoid every conflict and let resentment pile up; some meet every one at full strength and leave damage behind; most of us do both, depending on the day and the person.

Scripture assumes conflict will come, even among people who love God; the apostles had sharp disagreements, and Paul had to plead with two faithful women in Philippi to agree in the Lord. James names the deeper cause: we fight because we want things and do not get them. Pride hates to be wrong, fear hates to lose, and a sense of injury makes every word sound worse than it was meant. We are also very good at seeing the other person's speck and very poor at seeing our own beam. That does not mean every conflict is equally everyone's fault. It means that the first work in any conflict is usually our own.

So the Bible's wisdom refuses both the avoidance that buries the wound and the explosion that widens it. Begin with your own part, as Jesus said. Be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger, and answer gently even when you have to say something hard. Decide whether this is an offense to overlook, a matter to raise privately and honestly, or a wrong that belongs with someone in authority; harm and crime are never simply overlooked. Stay out of quarrels that are not yours, and refuse to carry gossip from one side to the other. Where the dispute is over something on which faithful people can differ, pursue peace and do not despise the other side. Where the other person will not make peace, sometimes the wise thing is Isaac's: make room, move on, and let God give the space.

The hope Scripture gives is that God is a peacemaker before we are, and that he blesses the peacemakers as his own children. In Christ he made peace with those who were his enemies, at his own cost, and he does not leave his people to make peace alone. Not every conflict will end in agreement, and not every person will be reconciled. But words that are true and full of grace are never wasted, and the one who seeks peace as far as it depends on them has done what God asks.
deep.sit: In the conflict you are carrying, what is the beam in your own eye, and what would a gentle, honest first word sound like?

prayer.lead: David's prayer for a guard over his mouth and a heart kept from evil. Pray it before a hard conversation.
prayer.text: Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch at the door of my lips. Do not let my heart be drawn to any evil thing or take part in works of wickedness with men who do iniquity; let me not feast on their delicacies.

careLines.text: If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true.
Tell someone you trust and get help.
Gentleness toward the one who fell never means carelessness toward the ones who were hurt.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
